items.title: How a war in Tigray could set off a more complex fight
items.description: For much of the past year, tensions between Ethiopia’s federal government and authorities in the northern Tigray region had been steadily escalating toward confrontation. The threat for those in Tigray, as much as for those in the wider region, was that the area could tip back into the kind of war that devastated the state between 2020 and 2022, but, this time, with a supercharged regional dimension. Officials in Addis Ababa and Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, have traded increasingly hostile accusations as the peace established at Pretoria frayed, while intermittent clashes and drone strikes produced episodes of serious violence. From the sidelines, Eritrea, Egypt, Somalia and Sudan — a pragmatic, loosely aligned anti-Ethiopia coalition — looked on. Then, on September 20, a drone struck a truck carrying more than 41 tons of food aid for displaced people in northwestern Tigray, setting the vehicle and its cargo ablaze. Aftermath of a drone strike on a humanitarian aid truck in northwestern Tigray, September 22. Courtesy: @JoeTseGy on X Three days later, Tigrayan forces seized three airports across the region. Fighting then spread beyond Tigray into neighboring Afar and Amhara. The federal government accused the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) of launching an offensive, while Tigrayan authorities said their forces were responding to federal attacks involving aircraft, drones, artillery and ground troops. Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Tigray after the airports were taken, while a Tigrayan official told Mada Masr that the confrontation has now become a “full war.” The fighting broke out only days after the TPLF joined six other armed organizations in the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Coalition for Survival. The members have pledged to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and establish a transitional administration. The coalition brought the TPLF together with the Amhara Fano National Movement, whose fighters had fought alongside federal forces against Tigray during the previous war, as well as the Oromo Liberation Army and movements from Ethiopia’s Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regions. Tigrayan and Amhara forces remain divided by unresolved claims over western and southern Tigray, making their decision to enter the same alliance one of the clearest signs of how Ethiopia’s domestic conflicts have been realigning since the end of the previous war. An Ethiopian political source who was close to the early discussions between several of the groups tells Mada Masr that contacts had been developing for roughly a year. The source says he lost interest as some of the participants established closer relationships with Sudan and what he had initially understood as a more political process moved, in his view, toward military coordination. Whatever the precise role played by those external relationships in bringing the alliance together, Ethiopian officials had already begun treating contacts between domestic armed opponents and neighboring states as parts of the same security problem. That concern had become increasingly public by May. After Ethiopian opposition figures and Eritrean officials met in Port Sudan under the banner of Tsimdo, army chief Berhanu Jula described what was taking shape as a “combined convergence” of Ethiopia’s adversaries. In June, Ethiopia’s foreign minister, Gedion Timothewos, predicted that an Eritrean-backed TPLF attack would come during the rainy season, while Abiy declared that, despite coordination between Sudan, Eritrea and Ethiopia’s armed groups, Ethiopia had “not an iota of fear.” In July, Abiy described an “axe politics” in which the TPLF formed the blade, Eritrea the wooden handle and an unnamed external actor the hand wielding it. The metaphor was polemical, but it reflected a security view in which domestic armed opposition, neighboring governments and contested borderlands were increasingly being read together. With the outbreak of fighting, which has shown no signs of abating since the end of last week, the question now is will the fighting remain confined to the Ethiopian interior or will the convergence of the last six months turn Ethiopia’s war into a new, complex regional fight to remake the Horn of Africa? … The significance of that convergence lies partly in the weakening of a regional hierarchy that for almost three decades gave Ethiopia greater freedom than most of its neighbors to operate across the Horn’s porous borders. After the upheavals of 1989-1991, Ethiopia emerged with the region’s strongest state and security apparatus and the greatest capacity to project influence into neighboring countries. Somalia collapsed and fragmented as its military regime came apart. Sudan retained a functioning center despite repeated peripheral wars. Eritrea became increasingly isolated since the mid-2000s, while Egypt’s direct role in the Horn diminished . Addis Ababa was consequently better placed than most of its neighbors to operate through their internal divisions without exposing its own to the same degree. That advantage has narrowed, while the means through which Addis Ababa seeks to preserve it have changed. Sudan’s political center has fractured into civil war, and Ethiopia itself has come to face armed movements across several regions. Eritrea has returned to active regional balancing, while Egypt has rebuilt relationships with states around Ethiopia, including deeper military and security cooperation with Somalia and closer ties with Eritrea and the Sudanese military-led authorities. Gulf states and other outside powers, meanwhile, operate not only through recognized governments but through ports, air routes, companies, armed groups and regional administrations. These relationships have not settled into stable blocs, and their participants can cooperate in one theater while competing in another, but they have made it easier for conflicts that once belonged to separate political arenas to feed into one another. “The region as it currently exists will not hold and should not hold,” Abiy recently told one foreign interlocutor. Many of those pressures intersect around Ethiopia. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) ties Addis Ababa to Egypt and Sudan through the Nile, while Ethiopia’s pursuit of sovereign maritime access has strained relations with Somalia and sharpened Eritrean concerns over the Red Sea. Tigray’s western frontier opens into Sudan, and the Fano insurgency runs through Amhara toward many of the same borderlands. Benishangul-Gumuz contains the GERD and faces Sudan’s Blue Nile State, where the civil war has moved toward Ethiopian territory, while Ethiopia’s agreement with Somaliland connected its search for the sea to Somali sovereignty disputes and Egyptian security policy in the Horn. Over the last six months, as the beat of the drum for an all out regional war has grown louder and louder, Mada Masr has spoken with Ethiopian military, intelligence and government officials, Sudanese officers and former diplomats, Tigrayan commanders and political figures, Eritrean sources close to decision-making circles and Egyptian officials, all of whom speak of how these theaters are being pulled together through Ethiopia’s changing regional position and vision for what the region should look like. What is clear is that Abiy does not see the status quo as a thing that is worth holding onto. “The region as it currently exists will not hold and should not hold,” he recently told one foreign interlocutor, who relayed the exchange to Mada Masr. That outlook has increasingly translated into an effort to use the Horn’s fragmented political geography to expand Ethiopia’s room for maneuver. Along the Sudanese frontier, that means treating territory beyond Ethiopia’s borders as strategic depth, from which threats to the federal state can be contained before they reach the center. On the Red Sea, it has meant dealing directly with Somaliland in pursuit of a maritime outlet, even when doing so cuts across Somalia’s claim to sovereignty. Tensions with Eritrea have brought the same ambition into the question of Assab, where Ethiopian demands for access to the sea increasingly collide with Eritrean concerns over sovereignty. From the signing of the memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland in 2024. Those moves have developed alongside a much closer relationship with the United Arab Emirates, which has given Addis Ababa access to investment, transport infrastructure and military technology at a time when Ethiopia’s own state capacity has been strained by internal war. Former Ethiopian officials describe that relationship as increasingly important not only to Abiy’s regional ambitions but to his effort to consolidate power at home. They also describe the search for Red Sea access as carrying a more personal political weight for the prime minister, who is looking for a defining achievement that can stand apart from the towering political legacy of former Ethiopian ruler Meles Zenawi. … The calculations now taking shape along Ethiopia’s borders reflect a change in the basis of the regional power Addis Ababa had accumulated after the upheavals of 1989–1991. During that period, Ethiopia was better placed to use the political divisions of neighboring states than its neighbors were to exploit Ethiopia’s own. The state Abiy inherited in 2018 had built that advantage through a powerful security apparatus and regional diplomatic clout under the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front, the coalition in which the TPLF had held the dominant position. That reach was reinforced by a post-September 11 international role that made Ethiopia a central partner for Washington during the so-called War on Terror. By the time Abiy took office, however, the domestic political settlement supporting that system was already coming apart. The Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), a TPLF-led coalition, ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018. Political scientists Harry Verhoeven and Michael Woldemariam, who interviewed a dozen senior Western and regional officials for a 2022 academic paper, described Ethiopia’s place in United States strategy during that period as that of an African “anchor state.” That meant an internationally backed role as regional enforcer and developmental leader, combined with an ability to influence political outcomes beyond its borders. The relationship did not create Ethiopia’s regional power, but it reinforced a system in which Addis Ababa’s diplomatic and security reach extended well beyond its immediate territory. The GERD added another dimension to that position, after construction began under Meles in 2011 in Benishangul-Gumuz, close to Sudan, placing an enormous Ethiopian infrastructure project on the river that supplies most of Egypt’s fresh water. Ethiopia presented the dam as a development project and an expression of its right to use Nile waters originating in its territory, while Cairo and Addis Ababa became locked in a dispute over its filling and operation and the implications for downstream water security. The project made a central part of its domestic development strategy inseparable from its regional position. The Blue Nile passes through the GERD, near Guba, Ethiopia, on December 26, 2019. Courtesy: Eduardo Soteras/AFP Abiy therefore came to power in April 2018 at the head of a state that still possessed much of this regional reach, even as the domestic political arrangement that had sustained it was breaking down. The EPRDF remained in government, but the internal hierarchy through which the TPLF had dominated the coalition was fraying after years of protest and repression. Abiy inherited the institutions and relationships of the old order but not the same political cohesion that had held them together. “I would fight and die for America.” Abiy’s familiarity with Washington predated his rise to the premiership. He had spent part of his earlier career inside Ethiopia’s intelligence and cyber-security apparatus, where his work brought him into contact with US security agencies. Reflecting on that period in a 2022 interview with The New Yorker, he said : “I was the one who would send intelligence from this part of the world to the N.S.A., on Sudan and Yemen and Somalia. The N.S.A. knows me. I would fight and die for America.” Verhoeven and Woldemariam argued that Washington consequently saw Abiy’s arrival in 2018 as an opportunity to reinvent its relationship with an indispensable regional partner, giving strong political support to a transition in which his domestic position remained much less settled. Abiy, in turn, presented himself as unusually compatible with Washington’s political and strategic preferences. He was more overtly religious than his secular left-wing predecessors, cultivated relationships with US political figures and signalled that Ethiopia under his leadership would be less dependent on China. Abiy Ahmed meets with former US Vice President Mike Pence. July 27, 2018 For Verhoeven and Woldemariam, that enthusiasm did more than legitimize Abiy’s transition. Washington’s strong backing, while Abiy’s position at home was still unsettled, made a more uncompromising effort to consolidate power seem less risky. In their account, the attempt to rebuild the US relationship with its Ethiopian anchor helped weaken the political settlement on which that relationship had depended. His first year brought substantial changes as the government released political prisoners, loosened restrictions on political and media activity, welcomed opposition figures back into the country and promised competitive elections, while also beginning to shift economic policy away from parts of the EPRDF’s state-led development model. Foreign governments responded enthusiastically, and Gulf states, with Washington’s encouragement, moved quickly to support the new leadership.. Abiy’s reconciliation with Eritrea appeared to extend that political opening across the region. Ethiopia and Eritrea had remained locked for almost two decades in the “no war, no peace” order that followed their 1998–2000 border war, until Abiy accepted the boundary ruling his predecessors had resisted and traveled to Asmara in July 2018 to restore relations with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki. The Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded him the Peace Prize the following year for his initiative in ending the stalemate with Eritrea and for broader efforts toward peace and international cooperation. For a period, those changes appeared to offer a way to renew Ethiopian regional leadership while rebuilding the political center at home, but the domestic project exposed a deeper disagreement over what should replace the old order. Most of the EPRDF and its allied regional parties were brought into the new Prosperity Party in late 2019, which Abiy and his supporters presented as a way to create a broader national political organization and weaken divisions embedded in the old coalition structure. The TPLF refused to join. Supporters regarded the new party as a means of strengthening national unity, while opponents feared greater centralization would come at the expense of regional autonomy and the multinational logic of Ethiopia’s federal system. The merger did not by itself cause the confrontation that followed, but it made the political rupture increasingly visible, as Tigray remained under the TPLF while its former coalition partners reorganized around Abiy in Addis Ababa. The dispute widened in 2020 after national elections were postponed during the COVID-19 pandemic and Tigray proceeded with its own regional vote, which the federal government rejected. By then, each side increasingly regarded the other as acting outside the constitutional order. War began in November 2020 and quickly drew in the Eritrean government, which had its own score to settle with the TPLF. Eritrean forces fought alongside the Ethiopian federal military and Amhara armed formations against a TPLF that Isaias had regarded as his principal regional enemy since the 1998–2000 war. Sudanese forces meanwhile moved into parts of disputed Fashaga as the fighting unfolded, while tens of thousands of refugees crossed into eastern Sudan. The Pretoria agreement, signed by the federal government, and the TPLF in November 2022 ended the principal war between them, providing for a cessation of hostilities, humanitarian access and a process of disarmament and restoration of federal authority. It did not reconstruct the political order that had preceded the conflict, and Eritrea was not a party to the agreement. Territorial disputes, the pace and terms of disarmament as well as Tigray’s relationship with the center remained contested, while tactical alliances produced by the war began to shift again. Ethiopian government representative Redwan Hussien and Tigray delegate Getachew Reda attend signing of the AU-led negotiations to resolve the conflict in northern Ethiopia, in Pretoria, South Africa, November 2, 2022. Courtesy: REUTERS/Siphiwe Sibeko Ethiopia emerged from the conflict with a diminished international position and a more fragmented domestic security environment, weakening the institutional basis of the regional role it had occupied during the EPRDF period, without necessarily eliminating its ability to project power beyond its borders. What had been damaged was the particular combination of domestic cohesion, Western backing and regional security relationships that had underpinned that position. The deterioration in Addis Ababa’s relationship with Washington was one measure of that loss. A former Kenyan ambassador tells Mada Masr that the US deepened its security ties with Nairobi during the same period, eventually making Kenya the first sub-Saharan African country to be designated a major non-NATO ally in 2024. Addis Ababa’s relationship with Washington, by contrast, deteriorated sharply during the Tigray war, including through restrictions on military cooperation and weapons-related sanctions that were only lifted in September. “Addis Ababa regards the restoration of military cooperation with Washington as part of a wider effort to rebuild state and military capacity.” A source in Ethiopia’s National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS) tells Mada Masr that Addis Ababa regards the restoration of military cooperation with Washington and the reopening of defense channels that were restricted during the Tigray war as part of a wider effort to rebuild state and military capacity. In the source’s account, the value of renewed cooperation extends beyond weapons to training, communications, reconnaissance, surveillance and logistical systems degraded by years of internal conflict. Reconstructing the institutional security relationship with Washington, the source says, is therefore seen in Addis Ababa as one means of recovering the ability to maneuver beyond Ethiopia’s borders rather than remain absorbed by internal wars. … Rebuilding the old relationship with Washington is only one part of that effort. Abiy has also sought to compensate for the erosion of the EPRDF-era architecture through a different set of relationships, relying more heavily on direct ties with foreign leaders, Gulf capital and military technology, and access to regional infrastructure that does not depend on the institutional channels through which Ethiopia exercised influence in the past. Abiy is haunted by the shadow of Meles Zenawi, a former senior Ethiopian official says. That search for a new basis of power has also become bound up with Abiy’s effort to distinguish his own political legacy from the era he inherited. “He is haunted by the shadow of Meles Zenawi,” a former senior Ethiopian official tells Mada Masr. He knows that the dam is, ultimately, Meles’s achievement, the official adds, arguing that Abiy is on a quest to find his own defining legacy. Crowds gather in mourning following the death of former Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi. August 22, 2012. Courtesy: AFP This quest has led the prime minister to embark on a brand of highly personalized politics, marked by distrust of traditional Ethiopian institutions, another former Ethiopian government official who spoke to Mada Masr in 2024 says. In the second former official’s account, major decisions have become concentrated around the prime minister and shaped through his relationships with individual foreign leaders, with the Foreign Ministry playing a smaller role in matters that would once have passed through established diplomatic channels. “Ethiopia’s relationship with the UAE increasingly brought Addis Ababa into a sphere where infrastructure carried security as well as commercial value.” The official argues that this made policy more dependent on personal relationships and more liable to abrupt shifts as Abiy sought investment, diplomatic backing and military capacity. The UAE has become one of the most important pillars of that newer architecture. Financial support from Abu Dhabi during the opening years of Abiy’s premiership developed alongside a much wider network of commercial, military and strategic interests across the Horn. The former Ethiopian official points particularly to Berbera and the transport connections running inland from Somaliland, arguing that Ethiopia’s relationship with the UAE increasingly brought Addis Ababa into a regional infrastructure in which ports, roads and investment carried security as well as commercial value. The attraction of maritime infrastructure grew as Abiy made Ethiopia’s lack of direct access to the sea an increasingly prominent national-security issue. For the first former Ethiopian official, returning Ethiopia’s direct access to the Red Sea was to be Abiy’s way of differentiating himself from his predecessor. In an October 2023 speech, he described the country as trapped in a “geographical prison” and argued that its growing population and economy could not remain indefinitely dependent on arrangements made through neighboring states. The memorandum signed with Somaliland on January 1, 2024 put that ambition into territorial form. Somaliland said the agreement would give Ethiopia access to 20 km of coastline while opening a path toward possible Ethiopian recognition of the territory’s claim to independence. A Somaliland read out said the agreement would hold for 50 years, while Ethiopia’s version said the agreement was permanent. Somalia rejected the arrangement as a violation of its sovereignty, while Ethiopia said its objective was to secure access to the sea rather than initiate a confrontation. Turkey-mediated talks later reduced the immediate confrontation between Addis Ababa and Mogadishu without resolving the strategic question that had produced it. Berbera remained important not only because it offered Ethiopia an alternative commercial and possible naval outlet, but because the port sits inside a wider UAE-linked network of infrastructure and security relationships across the Horn. Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan poses with Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed following a press conference in Ankara, Turkey, December 11, 2024. Courtesy: Reuters The Ethiopian NISS source says the government treats the search for a durable route to the sea as part of the same effort to rebuild Ethiopia’s regional position, with Addis Ababa seeking a long-term arrangement that would give it a stable maritime and commercial presence rather than leave access dependent on short-term political bargains. The source says Ethiopian institutions are also closely following emerging Red Sea security arrangements and want the country to move from being a landlocked state affected by decisions taken around the sea toward one that participates in shaping them. They add that discussions with regional and international actors have focused on ensuring Ethiopian interests in ports and trade routes are taken into account, while any eventual security role would center on coordination, information-sharing and the protection of commercial interests, rather than direct involvement in Yemen. … The regional importance of ports such as Berbera extends beyond Ethiopia’s own search for access to the sea. A former Sudanese diplomat who served in Addis Ababa describes large investments in ports, agriculture and transport as capable of acquiring “quasi-sovereign” characteristics where central governments exercise limited control, because the states and companies financing infrastructure can influence which routes function, where resources move and which local authorities benefit from them. In borderlands where formal authority already overlaps with armed groups, regional administrations and commercial networks, control over logistical and agricultural systems can therefore carry strategic weight alongside a conventional military presence. Alex de Waal, an author and veteran regional expert, places that process inside a wider transformation in the political geography of the Horn, which he tells Mada Masr has increasingly been integrated into the “commercial, security and political perimeter of the wider Middle East.” Arab states are central to that expansion, but Turkey, Israel and Iran also operate within it, bringing forms of competition developed across the Red Sea into political systems where authority has long extended unevenly beyond recognized capitals and borders. Sovereignty in the Horn is increasingly “sliced” territorially and “diced” into functions that were conventionally held together by a single state, de Waal says. The UAE, de Waal argues, has gone further than most in adapting to that environment. He describes Abu Dhabi as the region’s most developed “political marketplace” operator, building networks of patronage and influence according to the political and strategic value of particular actors, rather than the formal architecture of the states to which they belong. Abu Dhabi crown prince Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan walks with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed during Abiy’s visit to Abu Dhabi. January 29, 2022. Courtesy: Abdalla Al Neyadi/Ministry of Presidential Affairs/WAM via AP That strategy depends on the fragmentation of sovereignty itself in states that have historically struggled to exercise it across the full extent of their jurisdiction. De Waal describes sovereignty as increasingly “sliced” territorially, and “diced” into functions that were conventionally held together by a single state, allowing authority over defense, foreign relations, commerce or particular pieces of territory to be dealt with separately. The actors within that ecosystem built by the UAE can include recognized governments, such as Ethiopia, regional administrations, such as Puntland and Somaliland, and armed actors operating outside conventional state chains of command, like the Rapid Support Forces. They do not all serve the same function or operate in the same way, de Waal tells Mada Masr, but they are connected through logistics corridors, cash and personal relationships from which they all benefit. The commercial corridors built through those relationships can also carry military value because ports generate roads, warehouses, customs arrangements and transport systems that can move weapons, personnel and military technology as well as ordinary trade, he adds. The former Sudanese diplomat describes a regional geography increasingly organized around those systems, in which ostensibly commercial infrastructure can become one of the means through which military and geopolitical goals are pursued. When Ethiopia needed to mobilize this alternate geography for a specific goal, it was able stitch together roads, people and ports of different stripes. “Significant parts of the military leadership were kept unaware as the Assosa operation was built up,” says an Ethiopian military source. This is exactly what happened when Addis Ababa made the decision to throw its hat more decisively into the Sudan war. An Ethiopian military source tells Mada Masr that Somaliland’s Berbera Port has become a principal entry point for supplies destined for the RSF, with material moving overland through Ethiopia toward the Benishangul-Gumuz region. Berbera Port. Courtesy: Shutterstock An official at Ethiopian Shipping and Logistics and another at the Ethiopian Transport Ministry separately tell Mada Masr that a designated group of 10 company trucks had been used to move weapons through the country, while two Ethiopian military sources place the other end of the route around Assosa, close to Sudan’s Blue Nile frontier. The two military sources describe Assosa and the surrounding areas as part of a logistical system serving the RSF. The first Ethiopian military source says the Mao-Komo special district has been used for logistics and medical facilities. The source tells Mada Masr that the Ethiopian National Defense Forces base at Assosa supplied heavily armed vehicles to the RSF and forces allied with Abdel Aziz al-Hilu’s Sudan People’s Liberation Movement–North (SPLM-N) in their push to take the Sudanese city of Kurmuk. The development of that infrastructure also reflects the increasingly personalized security decision-making described by the second former Ethiopian government official. The second Ethiopian military source tells Mada Masr that significant parts of the military leadership were kept unaware as the Assosa operation was built up. The camp was developed secretly under Getachew Gudina, a senior intelligence commander, with close supervision from Abiy, the source says, adding that the military chief-of-staff did not become aware of the operation until the deployment stage, when equipment and logistical supplies began moving into place. In February, Reuters reported that Ethiopia was hosting a large camp in Benishangul-Gumuz where around 4,300 fighters were training for the RSF, drawing on satellite imagery, an Ethiopian security document and interviews with 15 sources. Several of those sources accused the UAE of financing the camp’s construction and said the recruits were expected to deploy toward Blue Nile, while the news agency also documented expansion at Assosa airport associated with drone operations. Ethiopia did not respond to Reuters’ questions about the camp, while the UAE denied financing or supporting the RSF. Across the border, Blue Nile was becoming more closely integrated into Sudan’s civil war as the RSF and Hilu’s SPLM-N faction pushed against Sudanese army positions around Yabus, Bau and Kurmuk. Hilu’s faction joined the RSF-aligned Tasis coalition after spending much of the earlier war outside the principal confrontation between the Sudanese military and the RSF, giving the latter experienced local forces in terrain adjoining Ethiopia and South Sudan. Sudanese officials have accused drones operating from the Ethiopian side of supporting those operations, allegations Addis Ababa has denied. The geography helps explain why activity around Assosa carries consequences beyond Blue Nile itself. Kurmuk, which has regularly changed hands between the RSF and the army, sits directly against the Ethiopian frontier, immediately west of Benishangul-Gumuz, while the GERD lies a short distance to the east. Farther north, the same frontier runs toward Fashaga and western Tigray, while roads and communities to the south connect Blue Nile to South Sudan. The route described by the Ethiopian transport and military sources runs from Berbera across Ethiopian transport networks toward Assosa and onward to the Sudanese border. The RSF was unusually well placed to operate through such a system because its own growth had occurred partly outside the conventional chain of state authority. It emerged from the Janjaweed militias used by the Sudanese government in Darfur before receiving formal recognition in 2013 and greater legal autonomy in 2017. Khartoum repeatedly assigned the force responsibilities in peripheral territories where the state had limited reach, while RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo later positioned the group inside the European Union-backed architecture for controlling migration along Sudan’s borders and deployed fighters to Yemen as part of the Saudi and Emirati-led coalition. Sudan researcher Sarra Majdoub described Hemedti in 2019 as a “governor” of the country’s margins, whose responsibilities across Darfur, Blue Nile and South Kordofan allowed him to accumulate political and economic power alongside his military role. She also called the RSF a “Frankenstein’s monster,” warning that the order that had empowered the force might eventually find itself threatened by it. By the time then-Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir was removed that year, Hemedti had already converted power accumulated on Sudan’s peripheries into an independent position with substantial foreign relationships of his own. Four years later, the RSF turned its weapons against the Sudanese army. The war greatly expanded those relationships into a logistical system stretching across neighboring states and commercial jurisdictions, making Assosa one component of a much larger network rather than a self-contained supply route. *** Ethiopia’s place within these relations is particularly consequential because the same permeability that can give the RSF access into Sudan can also give Ethiopian armed movements access to territory beyond the federal state’s control. A group of Tigrayan fighters, known as Army 70, operates from the Sudanese border. The force is made up of thousands of fighters and officers of Tigrayan origin who once served in Ethiopia’s federal armed forces before defecting or fleeing into Sudan after the outbreak of the Tigray war, a Sudanese source informed of the fighters movements previously told Mada Masr. In early August, Army 70 crossed from Sudan into Ethiopia and targeted Ethiopian military forces near the border area of Shererina. Earlier this year, when a Sudanese security attaché in Ethiopia spoke to Mada Masr, renewed war in the region remained a possibility rather than the reality it became in September. He described Tigray as a continuing vulnerability for the Ethiopian state because another political or military mobilization could draw on territory outside Ethiopian control, giving particular importance to the Sudan-facing crossings that could provide Tigrayan forces with external “logistical depth” in another confrontation with the center. “Ethiopia recognizes we’re no longer facing a fleeting disruption, but a comprehensive process of dismantling and reassembling the Sudanese state.” Several Sudanese sources describe the frontier from a different perspective, in which the breakdown of authority inside Sudan has created a vacuum for neighboring states and armed actors to operate through territories Khartoum can no longer regulate in the same way. “If you ask me what Ethiopia wants from Sudan at this defining moment and why it has intervened with all its weight [in the Sudan war],” a former senior Sudanese security and intelligence officer told Mada Masr earlier this year, “the answer lies in the fact that Addis Ababa, more than any other country, recognizes that we are no longer facing a fleeting disruption, but rather what I would call a comprehensive process of dismantling and reassembling the Sudanese state.” The era in which borders carried “the weight of rigid sovereignty,” he continued, was giving way to “a world of fluid borders and spaces.” In his account, that fragmentation has increased the leverage available to Addis Ababa around longstanding disputes over the Fashaga triangle and the GERD because influence can increasingly be exercised through local balances of power that Sudan’s central state is less able to manage. A former senior officer in Sudan’s eastern zone describes Fashaga, in more practical terms, as an area in which control is accumulated through cultivation of land, roads, rural infrastructure and security presence. During the Bashir era, an arrangement allowed Amhara farmers to cultivate land inside Sudan and return seasonally, but it broke down during the Tigray war when Sudan moved to halt incursions by Amhara militias accompanying Ethiopian farmers. Formal claims to sovereignty remain important, but the cost of reversing arrangements on the ground grows as communities, production and military positions become embedded in them, narrowing the distinction between economic activity and security control. For Tigrayan actors, the federal government’s concern over external “logistical depth” therefore appears in reverse. Access to Sudan is a “matter of life and death that transcends the calculations of temporary governments.” A prominent TPLF commander tells Mada Masr that weak central authority on the Sudanese side presented less of a threat to Tigray than an opening that could prevent the region from being sealed off. He argues that the Ethiopian government’s attempts to establish a lasting security cordon around Fashaga and Gadarif ran against much older social and logistical relationships crossing the frontier, and he describes Sudanese territory as Tigray’s principal source of strategic depth outside Ethiopia. Those relationships predate the present crisis by decades. During the struggle against the Derg in the 1970s and 1980s, Sudan provided Tigrayan fighters with refuge and served as a corridor for humanitarian and military supplies. The networks involved eastern Sudanese communities as well as regional governments, making them harder to eliminate through the closure of formal crossings alone. Federal security officials consequently regarded an open route into Sudan as one of the ways a renewed Tigrayan mobilization could acquire supplies and room for maneuver. The TPLF commander describes the same geography as protection against isolation, calling access to Sudan a “matter of life and death that transcends the calculations of temporary governments.” Those competing views of the frontier were recorded before the September fighting again turned the question of Tigray’s external access from a contingency into an immediate security concern. … Ethiopia’s effort to acquire maritime access produced another series of reactions to the east. Somalia treated the 2024 memorandum between Ethiopia and Somaliland as a challenge to its territorial integrity and deepened its relationship with Cairo as its dispute with Addis Ababa intensified. Egypt and Somalia signed a military cooperation protocol in August 2024, after which Egyptian military aircraft delivered weapons and ammunition to Mogadishu, while Cairo later offered forces for the African Union mission that succeeded the African Union Transmission Mission in Somalia (ATMIS). Ethiopian officials increasingly interpreted those relationships less as support for Somalia and more as an attempt to constrain Ethiopia. Redwan Hussein, Ethiopia’s intelligence chief, accused Cairo of acting from “animosity toward Ethiopia,” while Ethiopia’s ambassador to Somalia later described Egypt’s regional posture in the language of “encirclement.” Cairo describes its expansion of regional relationships through a different security logic, in which the Horn has become increasingly important because the issues of Nile water security, Red Sea navigation and approaches to the Suez Canal intersect there. “Cairo treats the region as a form of strategic depth to protect interests that can no longer be addressed through the Nile dispute alone.” An Egyptian official responsible for the Horn file tells Mada Masr that Cairo consequently treats the region as a form of strategic depth, with relationships in Somalia, Eritrea, Sudan and Djibouti intended to protect interests that can no longer be addressed through the Nile dispute alone. The official describes Ethiopia as the principal state-level challenge to Egyptian interests within that system, while acknowledging that Egypt has fewer financial resources than Gulf states capable of using investment, infrastructure and patronage across the region on a much larger scale. Cairo’s effort has therefore relied heavily on state-to-state security relationships, military cooperation and diplomatic coordination with governments whose own disputes with Addis Ababa have intensified. Somaliland’s former president, Muse Bihi, who signed the recognition-for-sea-access agreement with Ethiopia, later identified Egypt as the principal external actor behind efforts that ultimately thwarted the arrangement. Whatever weight is given to Bihi’s account, the dispute demonstrated how quickly Ethiopia’s maritime ambitions could become entangled with the much older Egyptian-Ethiopian confrontation over regional power and the Nile. And once the sea-access agreement with Somaliland was pushed to the side, Ethiopia turned its sights to Eritrea. In a September 2025 speech near the GERD, Abiy described the loss of access to Assab as a mistake made three decades ago, referring to Eritrea’s 1993 independence from Ethiopia. “The mistake took place yesterday and will be corrected tomorrow,” Abiy told the gathered crowd. “Well, the question of Eritrea’s independence isn’t really settled yet, is it?” While the prime minister later publicly backed away from the suggestion that he would “reclaim” Assab, a Western diplomatic source says the messaging coming from Ethiopian officials over the past two years has been: “well, the question of Eritrea’s independence isn’t really settled yet, is it?” For Asmara, this line of talk in public and behind closed doors has raised concerns. “We view Ethiopia’s declared and implicit rhetoric and ambitions to secure a sovereign maritime outlet, particularly the repeated hints regarding Eritrea’s Port of Assab, as an existential threat and a direct infringement on Eritrean sovereignty that can’t be tolerated. We consider it a broad red line, and crossing it or any unilateral Ethiopian military move toward Eritrean borders would ignite a direct and full-scale confrontation,” an Eritrean source close to decision-making says. The increasingly tense Eritrean-Ethiopian relations created an opening for Egypt. Eritrea occupies a particularly important place in Cairo’s calculations because, as the Egyptian official puts it, its geography connects the Nile, the Red Sea and the Horn, and its long coastline gives it importance to Red Sea navigation, while its border with Ethiopia gives it direct strategic relevance to a state with which Egypt remains divided over the GERD. The official describes closer relations with Asmara as part of a wider effort to prevent any one regional actor from acquiring overwhelming influence across both the Nile Basin and the Horn. Those relationships had acquired a public diplomatic structure by October 2024, when President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Afwerki and Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud met in Asmara. The declaration that came out of their meeting emphasized sovereignty and territorial integrity and established a tripartite foreign-ministerial committee for strategic cooperation. Following the summit, a separate Egyptian-Somali declaration reaffirmed support for Somalia’s territorial unity and closer cooperation with its state institutions. The summit did not announce an alliance against Ethiopia, but it brought together three governments whose relations with Addis Ababa had all become more difficult as Ethiopia pressed its maritime claims and its dispute with Cairo over the Nile continued. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki and Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud meet in Asmara. October 10, 2024 The Eritrean source close to decision-making circles describes the rapprochement with Egypt in more explicitly security-focused terms, calling it a “comprehensive strategic restructuring” intended to adjust the balance of power in the Horn and Red Sea. The source says Eritrea sought Egyptian assistance to improve military readiness and technical capacity after concluding that the Sudan war, Ethiopia’s internal conflicts and renewed tensions over maritime access were becoming increasingly difficult to treat as separate threats. Sudan also forms part of that relationship, in the source’s account, with security and intelligence coordination among Asmara, Cairo and the Sudanese military-led authorities developing alongside Eritrean support for forces aligned with the Sudanese military. Accounts differ over the extent of Egypt’s physical military presence in Eritrea. The Eritrean source says cooperation is concentrated on training, military modernization and intelligence coordination. “The idea is not to fight. The idea is to send a message to Ethiopia and the UAE.” Cairo is working to improve its military position in the area, an informed Egyptian state official says. “The idea is not to fight. The idea is to send a message to Ethiopia and the UAE that we have a strong presence around Ethiopia,” they add. The first Egyptian official echoes the flexible contours of the cooperation, saying that military and security coordination operates through understandings between the leaderships and the agencies involved. Several Egyptian officials who spoke to Mada Masr in recent months downplayed the possibility that Egyptian troops would become involved in the fight. However, one Egyptian state official underlined that logistical and military support is already being set in motion and would continue. … As those state-level pressures have accumulated, Ethiopia’s domestic armed movements have acquired greater regional value without ceasing to be products of conflicts rooted inside Ethiopia. But that growing regional value has not made those armed movements mere products of the governments seeking relationships with them. Tigray’s confrontation with the federal government grew out of the collapse of the political order that had governed Ethiopia since 1991 and the war that began in 2020, while Fano’s mobilization followed a different history rooted in Amhara protest politics, insecurity, territorial claims and a wartime alliance with the federal government that later broke down. The two movements arrived at their present confrontation with Addis Ababa through different political trajectories and retain disagreements that the alliance announced in September has not resolved as a starting point. Tigray People’s Liberation Front forces. Courtesy: AFP/Yasuyoshi Chiba Tigrayan politics itself had fractured in the years after the Pretoria agreement, as rival political camps sought accommodation with governments that had fought against the region during the previous war. A faction associated with TPLF head Debretsion Gebremichael rebuilt contacts with Eritrea, while figures associated with Getachew Reda, the former head of Tigray’s interim regional administration and current minister advisor to Abiy on East African affairs, pursued a more accommodating relationship with Addis Ababa. The realignments were particularly striking because Eritrean forces had bitterly fought the TPLF during the war, while Amhara forces fought alongside the federal government and took control of territories claimed by Tigrayan political forces. Fano had meanwhile become one of the principal armed challengers to the same federal government alongside which its fighters had acquired much of their expanded military capacity. After Pretoria, Addis Ababa moved to dismantle regional and irregular armed structures, while Amhara actors feared that disarmament would weaken their position in territories captured during the conflict. The wartime reliance on Amhara armed formations had strengthened organizations outside the regular federal chain of command before the alliance between them and Addis Ababa collapsed. “More than 85 percent of Amhara Regional State’s territory is controlled by Fano, while government forces are highly squeezed in the zonal cities,” Eyob Tilahun, an Ethiopian academic with close contacts with the Fano fighters, tells Mada Masr. “Fano forces frequently attack even major zonal cities and the regional capital.” The process through which Fano became a force bears some resemblance to the trajectory through which the Sudanese state empowered the RSF, although the organizations emerged from very different political and institutional histories. Bashir’s government formally built up the RSF over years and granted it autonomous coercive, economic and political capacity, while Fano remained considerably more dispersed and less institutionalized. In both cases, however, governments struggling to exercise coercive control across contested peripheral territories helped strengthen armed actors that later pursued increasingly autonomous goals. Their subsequent search for outside relationships does not make either Fano or Tigrayan factions simple proxies for neighboring governments. Fano’s territorial demands and claims of insecurity predate the current regional alignment, while Tigrayan actors understand access to Sudan through a history stretching back to the struggle against the Derg. What has changed is the strategic value those conflicts can acquire for governments seeking leverage over Addis Ababa, since an armed movement capable of opening another internal Ethiopian front can become useful to an external actor even where their political projects remain incompatible. The contacts that eventually developed into the alliance announced in September moved through several channels without resolving those incompatibilities. An Ethiopian source close to the Fano armed group tells Mada Masr that one purpose of the Tsimdo initiative hosted in Port Sudan in May was to facilitate contacts between Tigrayan and Eritrean actors through Sudanese mediation. By August, Fano commander Zemene Kassie was publicly describing relations with several Ethiopian opposition movements, including Tigrayan actors, as the beginnings of wider cooperation. By September 21, seven armed organizations had formalized that cooperation in the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Coalition for Survival. Their common opposition to Addis Ababa did not resolve disputes carried over from the previous war. Wolqayt and other parts of western and southern Tigray remain claimed by Amhara and Tigrayan political forces, leaving one of the conflict’s most consequential territorial questions inside the alliance itself. A senior Somali official tells Mada Masr that this kind of political order is better understood through overlapping networks whose participants can cooperate in one theater while competing in another. Turkey has defended Somali territorial sovereignty and developed deep military ties with Mogadishu while maintaining important economic and military relations with Addis Ababa. Somali officials were able to use Ankara’s relationships on both sides to help defuse their dispute with Ethiopia. But those same overlapping ties also place limits on how far Mogadishu can push the confrontation, the source says. Despite broader concern about Ethiopia’s rapidly changing regional posture, Somalia’s own security relationship with Addis Ababa due to mutual concerns about Al-Shabab makes a more aggressive stance difficult to sustain. … And while all these overlapping networks can take on an air of abstraction — through diplomatic gossip of who is talking to whom as all sides try to adopt the right posture — nothing better establishes how this comes to a head than the border area itself. In late August, Hemedti traveled quietly to Addis Ababa as fighting intensified in Blue Nile State. A source in the RSF leadership and an Ethiopian official told Mada Masr at the time that operations and troop movements along the border were among the subjects discussed during the visit. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed receives RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo at a restaurant in Addis Ababa. Courtesy: Ethiopian Prime Minister on X An ENDF source and a Benishangul-Gumuz security source tell Mada Masr that Hemedti traveled onward to Assosa, where he consulted RSF and Ethiopian military officers at the Bamboo Hotel. Field Marshal Berhanu Jula, General Abebaw Tadesse and military intelligence chief Getachew Gudina traveled to Assosa several weeks earlier for meetings with regional security officials and ENDF commanders, the sources add. RSF presence has become more entrenched around an ENDF site near Fana Mountain, where they are developing a drone operations center. Those meetings took place amid a broader military buildup around Assosa. The Benishangul-Gumuz security source says that the RSF presence had become more entrenched around an ENDF site near Fana Mountain, where they are developing a drone operations center alongside facilities capable of handling military aircraft. The source describes foreign personnel and local irregular forces operating around the site. Airports at Assosa and Bahir Dar are also being used to stage drone operations, a high-ranking Ethiopian Air Force official tells Mada Masr. At the Ethiopian Air Force Headquarters in Debre Zeit, Emirati colonels are stationed under special security protection to oversee drone operations, the source adds, while close to 30 Ethiopian military personnel have been sent to the UAE to train in drone operation. While the equipment that been flown and shipped into northern Ethiopia in the last month ahead of Hemedti’s visit to the base will be made available in part to the RSF, the Ethiopian Air Force source says that the focus on drone capacity has mostly been in preparation for war with Tigray and ongoing fighting with Fano. … The Sudanese military-led authorities were building relationships of their own as military activity around the Ethiopian frontier increased. Burhan traveled to Asmara on September 4 for talks with Afwerki, describing the visit as part of continuing consultations between Sudan and Eritrea and thanking Asmara for what he called its “consistent stance.” The visit placed the leader of the Sudanese military in Eritrea only days after the head of the force fighting him had reportedly been in Ethiopia. On September 17, Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council Deputy Chair Malik Agar, originally from Blue Nile State, said Khartoum does not want to enter a war with Ethiopia, even as senior Sudanese military officers were accusing Addis Ababa of allowing RSF drones to operate from Ethiopian territory. Two days earlier, Sudanese military chief-of-staff Yasser al-Atta accused Ethiopia of exploiting Sudan’s civil war to take border territory and permitting RSF drone launches as attacks struck Blue Nile. Ethiopia had rejected earlier Sudanese allegations of involvement as baseless. Hemedti’s movement toward Addis Ababa and Assosa, Burhan’s visits to Asmara and the sharpening dispute between Sudan and Ethiopia gave visible form to alignments that still fell short of two disciplined military blocs. Eritrea and the Sudanese military-led authorities have reasons to avoid a wider interstate conflict, while the extent of Egyptian military involvement remains calibrated, and, in some areas, ambiguous. The Ethiopian opposition alliance is itself held together across political and territorial disagreements capable of resurfacing even as its members confront a common federal adversary. The events of late September nevertheless showed that those contradictions do not prevent tactical relationships from acquiring military consequences. Two days after the alliance was announced, the confrontation in northern Ethiopia expanded across Tigray, Afar and Amhara as Tigrayan forces seized the airports that had connected the region to the rest of the country. The renewed conflict therefore began at a moment when the actors around Ethiopia were more densely connected to one another than they had been when the Pretoria agreement ended the previous war. The permeability through which those relationships operate belongs to a much longer history of the Horn. De Waal has compared the states of the region to trees whose branches grow across one another because the effective political reach of governments and armed movements has rarely ended at recognized borders. The upheavals around 1989–1991 were themselves produced partly through insurgencies, governments and external patrons operating across those boundaries, and the regional order that followed did not eliminate those practices so much as arrange them around a hierarchy in which Ethiopia enjoyed greater capacity than most of its neighbors to manage them. What has changed is less the existence of cross-border alliances and proxy relationships and more the infrastructure available to sustain them. The branches extending across the Horn now carry drones and air bridges, commercial ports and transport companies, foreign contractors, financial networks and sub-state authorities alongside the rebel movements and intelligence services familiar from earlier periods. Geographic permeability is old, while the density and technological capacity of the systems operating through it are newer. The post How a war in Tigray could set off a more complex fight first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: La ligue régionale de basketball de Gao a un nouveau président
items.description: Abdoul Malick Diallo prend la tete de la Ligue regionale de basketball de Gao pour un mandat de quatre ans. Il a ete elu ce mercredi 30 septembre avec 2 voix sur les 3 exprimees , lors d'une assemblee tenue a la direction regionale de la jeunesse et des sports. Il succede a Abdoulaye Bocoum. Le nouveau president entend notamment renforcer la pratique du basketball, accompagner les clubs et favoriser l'emergence de jeunes talents dans la region. L’article La ligue régionale de basketball de Gao a un nouveau président est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Tennessee : une condamnée à mort survit à deux injections létales
items.description: Christa Pike, condamnée à mort pour le ⁠meurtre d'une camarade ​de classe il y a 30 ans, a survécu à la tentative de l'État du Tennessee de l'exécuter par injection létale mercredi soir. Une enquête a été ouverte et les exécutions sont suspendues dans le Tennessee. De son côté, l'ONU appelle à renoncer à une nouvelle tentative d'exécution.

items.title: RDC: un membre de Médecins sans frontières infecté par Ebola évacué vers les Pays-Bas
items.description: Un membre du personnel de Médecins sans frontières (MSF) engagé dans la riposte contre Ebola en RDC a été évacué ce jeudi 1er octobre vers les Pays-Bas. MSF confirme une infection au virus Bundibugyo. Selon le ministre congolais de la Santé, Roger Kamba, interrogé par RFI, cet expatrié européen dont la nationalité n'a pas été révélée a été contaminé dans la zone de Beni, au Nord-Kivu. Cette évacuation intervient alors que le pays comptait près de 4 000 décès au 29 septembre.

items.title: Pourquoi Trump refuse de ralentir le développement de l’IA
items.description: Selon une étude présentée le 25 septembre, l'investissement cumulé aux États-Unis dans les infrastructures de l'intelligence artificielle pourrait atteindre 10 300 milliards de dollars sur la période 2025-2032, soit 3,6 % du PIB en moyenne chaque année. À la fin de cette période, en 2032, ces investissements représenteraient 5,1 % du PIB Financing the AI Buildout , Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, 25 septembre 2026.'> 59 . C'est près de 2 points de plus que les dépenses de défense, estimées à 3,2 % du PIB en 2026 The $8 trillion arms surge fuelling AI — and spooking bonds », Reuters , 30 septembre 2026.'> 60 . Le boom de l’intelligence artificielle est sans commune mesure avec les investissements réalisés lors des précédents grands cycles d'infrastructures aux États-Unis. Les chemins de fer avaient représenté en moyenne 2,2 % du PIB par an entre 1870 et 1890, l'électrification 0,5 % entre 1905 et 1925, les autoroutes 1,1 % entre 1956 et 1973, et la fibre et les télécommunications 1,1 % sur la période 1996-2003. Ces investissements serviront à construire les infrastructures physiques nécessaires au développement de la technologie : centres de données (bâtiments, systèmes de refroidissement), infrastructures électriques de raccordement et, pour environ les deux tiers, matériel informatique. Les hyperscalers consacrent en effet des sommes considérables à l'achat de puces, dont la durée de vie économique est pourtant estimée à cinq ou six ans. Les grandes entreprises technologiques américaines ne peuvent pas assumer seules ces financements. Plus de la moitié proviendra ainsi de capitaux extérieurs (investisseurs en fonds propres, marchés obligataires, banques et crédit privé), ce qui a pour conséquence de disperser les risques potentiels à travers le système financier, jusqu'aux fonds de pension AI's never-before-seen capital grab », Axios , 24 septembre 2026.'> 61 . Selon une analyse de deux économistes de Stanford, Jared Bernstein et Ryan Cummings, pour rentabiliser les investissements dans l'IA réalisés depuis 2024 par Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle et SpaceX, ces entreprises devraient générer entre 2 400 et 3 800 milliards de dollars de revenus tirés de l'IA sur les six prochaines années, ce qui suppose une multiplication de leurs revenus actuels liés à l'IA par 13 à 45 AI Companies Are In a Race Against Time , 25 septembre 2026.'> 62 . Les retours sur investissement pourraient toutefois se concrétiser plus tardivement qu’anticipé. Berstein et Cummings écrivent : « La diffusion d’une nouvelle technologie exige non seulement que les entreprises l’adoptent, mais aussi qu’elles déterminent comment l’intégrer au mieux dans leurs processus de travail existants, un processus qui peut prendre un temps considérable. Par exemple, en 1900, seuls 5 % de la puissance mécanique étaient électrifiés. Il a fallu attendre encore 30 ans pour atteindre un taux d’adoption de 80 % ». Donald Trump considère que la domination américaine de l’IA pourrait constituer l’un des principaux héritages de son second mandat. Mardi 29 septembre, à la Maison-Blanche, il a fait signer par OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI et Nvidia un accord par lequel ces entreprises s'engagent volontairement à s'autoréguler. Le document se contente d'évoquer la possibilité, « à terme », d'inscrire ces engagements dans la loi ou la réglementation. L’article Pourquoi Trump refuse de ralentir le développement de l’IA est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .
